basics.name: Japanese joinery catalogues and tools: The Complete Japanese Joinery (Hideo Sato and Yasuo Nakahara, trans. Koichi Paul Nii), The Art of Japanese Joinery (Kiyosi Seike), The Joinery 3D GIF animations (@TheJoinery_jp on X/Twitter) and Tsugite (Larsson, Yoshida, Umetani and Igarashi, University of Tokyo, UIST 2020)
basics.url: No single home page. Sato and Nakahara book record: https://archive.org/details/completejapanese0000unse (Open Library edition OL22474514M, with table of contents); Seike book record: https://archive.org/details/artofjapanesejoi0000seik (Open Library edition OL4542211M); The Joinery animations: https://x.com/thejoinery_jp; Tsugite code: https://github.com/marialarsson/tsugite (paper DOI 10.1145/3379337.3415899, metadata and abstract checked at https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1145/3379337.3415899?fields=title,year,abstract,citationCount,openAccessPdf,venue,authors)
basics.resource_type: book (two illustrated catalogues of traditional Japanese wood joints) + video/animation collection (The Joinery GIFs on X) + interactive tool (Tsugite, a research prototype desktop app on GitHub)
basics.cost: Sato and Nakahara: paid, paperback about USD 29.95 new (Lake Forest Book Store listing), cheaper used; free to borrow from Internet Archive's lending library. Seike: paid, about USD 29.95 new (William Stout Architectural Books listing), also borrowable on Internet Archive. The Joinery GIFs: free to view on X (a free X login may be needed to scroll the full history). Tsugite: free for personal use and non-commercial research; commercial use needs a licence from the University of Tokyo TLO (README)
basics.license: Both books: all rights reserved (commercial publishers), so link to the records and do not copy the drawings. The Joinery GIFs: no licence stated, so treat as all rights reserved and link or embed the posts rather than re-hosting them [uncertain]. Tsugite: the README says 'free for personal use and non-commercial research conducted within non-commercial organizations' and the repo's LICENSE file is the GNU Free Documentation License 1.3; commercial use needs permission. The ACM paper is copyrighted by ACM/authors
basics.language: English (both books are English translations of Japanese originals; Seike's is a translation of 'Kigumi'). The Joinery posts give each joint's Japanese name in kanji plus a romanised (romaji) name. Tsugite: English interface and README
basics.year: Seike, The Art of Japanese Joinery: first English edition 1977 (John Weatherhill / Tankosha), still in print (reprinted; a 2025 reprint is mentioned by booksellers [uncertain]). Sato and Nakahara, The Complete Japanese Joinery: 1995 (Hartley & Marks, Point Roberts WA), paperback reprint 1 June 2000. The Joinery account: joined February 2016, GIFs posted mainly 2016 to February 2017 (latest post seen 25 Feb 2017). Tsugite: UIST 2020 paper; the repo README targets Python 3.8.3 and pip 21.1.2 (about 2021) [uncertain]
basics.access_barrier: Books: paywall (buy) or free Internet Archive login to borrow (the scans are access-restricted lending copies, not open downloads). The Joinery: none to view the profile; X may ask for a free login to scroll or view older posts. Tsugite: desktop install (Python 3.8 with packages from requirements.txt, then run tsugite_app.py) plus a 3-axis CNC mill to make the joints
basics.image_license: Book figures and photographs: all rights reserved. The Joinery GIFs: all rights reserved by the creator (press articles such as Dezeen credit 'Imagery courtesy of The Joinery and Spoon & Tamago') [uncertain]. Tsugite README images: covered by the repo's non-commercial terms and GFDL LICENSE file [uncertain]
basics.authority_level: Books: educator/professional (Seike was Professor of Architecture at Tokyo Institute of Technology; Sato and Nakahara are Japanese carpentry authorities [uncertain]). The Joinery: community/unvetted (a hobbyist working in automobile marketing who redrew joints from his collection of woodwork books). Tsugite: academic peer-reviewed (ACM UIST 2020, University of Tokyo)

coverage.covers: Traditional Japanese interlocking wood joints that hold without nails, screws or glue. Sato and Nakahara (397 pages) is the broadest: tools and their care, wood, layout, then chapters on tsugite (end-to-end splice joints, p.173), shiguchi (right-angle joints, p.196), 'various types of fasteners' (wooden pegs, wedges and keys, p.205), framing, floors, roof framing and hip rafters, plus a glossary; it is often said to hold several hundred joints [uncertain]. Seike (128 pages) presents 48 joints chosen from the several hundred in use, with isometric drawings and 64 pages of photographs. The Joinery has about 80 to 105 animated GIFs (Dezeen, October 2016, said 80; the X profile now shows 105 posts), each one joint shown sliding together. Tsugite is not a catalogue but a design tool: it models any joint on a voxel grid (end-to-end, L and T type frame joints), checks it, offers a gallery of valid pre-computed joints and exports CNC milling paths
coverage.organisation: Sato and Nakahara: by function, then by building part (end joints, right-angle joints, fasteners, framing, floors, roofs); uses Japanese category terms with English glosses (e.g. 'Tsugite—End Joints', 'Shiguchi—Right Angle Joints'). Seike: a curated gallery of 48 joints with history. The Joinery: a chronological social media feed; each post is titled only with the kanji and romanised Japanese name, so it is hard to browse for someone who does not know the terms (names end in -tsugi for splices and -shikuchi for corner joints, which is the only built-in grouping). Tsugite: interactive, with a manual edit mode and a gallery mode filtered by validity
coverage.scope_match: low to medium: these are clever self-locking interlocking joints, which fit the 'clever connection types' idea, but they are woodwork/CNC joinery, which the project ranks lower priority; useful mainly for the short list of interlocking joints and as a visual presentation model
coverage.taxonomy_used: Japanese carpentry scheme with two main joint groups: tsugite (end/splice joints that lengthen a member) and shiguchi (joints where members meet at an angle), plus fasteners (sen pegs, kusabi wedges, shachi keys) as a separate group; Sato and Nakahara then organise by building element. Joint names are compositional: shape (ari = dovetail, kama = gooseneck, hozo = tenon, aikaki = halving) + locking device (sen = peg, shachi-sen = draw key) + group (tsugi or shikuchi). Tsugite classifies by joint topology (I, L, T, X arrangements of two to four timbers) and by sliding direction [uncertain]
coverage.example_types: Gooseneck splice (kama tsugi; 'Yonmai-kama-tsugi' four-piece gooseneck, 'Sumi-nihou-kama-tsugi'); dovetail splice and dovetail housing ('Yose-ari-hozo-shikuchi', 'Shinozashi-ari-shikuchi', 'Ari-gata-sashi-gumi-shikuchi'); four-way tenon splice ('Shihou-hozo-tsugi'); halved box joint locked with a draw-key ('Hako-aikaki-shachi-sen-shikuchi'); through double tenon locked with a through-peg ('Toshi-chigai-hozo-sashi-hanasen-shikuchi'); loose (inserted) tenon joint ('Yatoi-hozo-sashi-shikuchi'); 'Kai-no-kuchi-tsugi' (shell-mouth splice); scissor-like balanced interlock ('Kohibi-tenbin-kumi-tsugi'); four-sided hooked scarf ('Hagata-shimen-isuka-tsugi'); hidden-line double-tenon splice ('Kakushi-meji-nimai-hozo-tsugi'); fan-shaped tenon splice ('Ougi-hozo-tsugi'); stepped double-tenon cross joint ('Watari-ago-niju-hozo-shikuchi'). (Names verified in The Joinery posts quoted by Dezeen, ArchDaily and the X profile; the plain-English glosses are the researcher's own [uncertain])
coverage.making_methods: Hand-tool woodwork and timber framing (both books); CAD animation (The Joinery used Autodesk Fusion 360); 3-axis CNC milling (Tsugite, with corner rounding so milled parts still slide together)
coverage.item_count: Seike: 48 joints. The Joinery: about 80 GIFs by October 2016 and 105 posts on the profile now. Sato and Nakahara: 397 pages with joint chapters from p.173 to p.366 (exact joint count not verified) [uncertain]. Tsugite: an open-ended design space rather than a fixed list
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Self-locking: yes, many joints lock by their shape plus a driven peg, wedge or draw key (ArchDaily describes the set as 'some self-locking'). Hand-release only / knock-down: partly, since pegged and keyed joints can be taken apart by knocking the peg out, but this is not labelled [uncertain]. One-way sliding: Tsugite explicitly checks 'slidability' (that the parts can slide together in exactly one direction and lock). Torque-limiting, ratchet, detent, over-centre, compliant, print-in-place, gear trains, powered connectors and adhesives: not covered (these joints deliberately avoid glue)
coverage.entry_structure: Books: joint name (Japanese and English), isometric exploded drawing, photographs, use in a building, cutting and layout method (Sato and Nakahara add step-by-step layout and tool technique). The Joinery: one looping animated GIF per post with the kanji and romaji name only, no text explanation or dimensions. Tsugite: an editable 3D voxel joint with live feedback (slidability, fabricability, durability with regard to fibre direction), up to four suggested fixes, a .tsu save file and CNC milling path export
coverage.audience_level: Books: hobbyist to professional woodworker and carpenter (Seike's publisher says even weekend carpenters can copy the joints); The Joinery: general public and hobbyists; Tsugite: research / advanced maker with a CNC mill

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: medium: The Joinery animations are the most beginner-friendly way to see how an interlocking joint slides together, but the posts use only Japanese names; Seike is a gentle illustrated introduction; Sato and Nakahara is dense and uses Japanese carpentry terms; Tsugite needs Python setup and CNC knowledge
usefulness.has_images: yes: both books have clear isometric line drawings (Seike adds 64 pages of photographs); The Joinery has clean shaded 3D renders; Tsugite README has interface screenshots
usefulness.has_animations: yes: The Joinery is a set of looping animated GIFs (made in Fusion 360) showing each joint sliding together, widely reshared by Dezeen, ArchDaily, Boing Boing and others; Tsugite has an interactive 3D editor and a UIST 2020 presentation video on YouTube [uncertain]. The books are static
usefulness.gaps: No plain-English names or grouping by what the joint does; no strength numbers, clearances or fits for the maker's materials; nothing on 3D printing (tolerances for printed dovetails, for example); The Joinery gives no text, dimensions or source book for each joint and has not posted since 2017; books are paid and not openly online; Tsugite is a research prototype with no support and needs a CNC mill
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: partly: individual X posts have stable per-post URLs (e.g. https://x.com/thejoinery_jp as the profile; individual status URLs exist but none were opened), though X may require login and posts can vanish. Book records are stable (https://archive.org/details/completejapanese0000unse) but are whole-book, not per-joint. Tsugite repo link (https://github.com/marialarsson/tsugite) is fine as a single 'design your own joint' link
usefulness.reusable_data: not reusable as data: the books and GIFs are all rights reserved and scrape-only; joint names can be reused as facts. The Open Library record gives a machine-readable table of contents. Tsugite code is available but only for personal and non-commercial research use
usefulness.maintained: Books: in print (Seike reprinted; Sato and Nakahara available new). The Joinery: account online (37.8K followers) but inactive since early 2017. Tsugite: repo online; the README still says the wiki manuals are 'coming soon', so it looks unmaintained since about 2021 [uncertain]; follow-on research continues (MiGumi, SIGGRAPH Asia 2025, makes 30 traditional joints CNC-millable)
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: One short looping animation per joint showing the parts sliding together and locking (The Joinery's format is the single most shared way these joints have been explained). Compositional naming: break a name into shape + locking device + group, and teach those few root words (ari = dovetail, kama = gooseneck, sen = peg, tsugi = splice, shikuchi = corner). Split joints into 'lengthening' (end-to-end) and 'meeting at an angle' groups. Tsugite's live checks (can it slide together? can it be made with a round cutter? is the grain strong here?) could become flow-chart questions
usefulness.design_rules_given: Books: layout and cutting proportions for timber framing (not verified in detail) [uncertain]. The Joinery: none. Tsugite: qualitative checks rather than numbers (slidability, fabricability, fibre-direction durability) and corner rounding based on the milling bit radius; no clearances or strengths
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: yes for Tsugite: a voxel-grid joint editor with a gallery of pre-computed valid joints and automatic 3-axis CNC toolpath generation; the books and GIFs are not parametric
usefulness.file_formats: Books: print (and Internet Archive controlled-lending scans). The Joinery: animated GIF / video posts. Tsugite: its own .tsu joint file plus exported CNC milling paths (G-code format not verified) [uncertain]
usefulness.terminology_value: high for Japanese joint names: the books and The Joinery give standard kanji and romanised names (tsugite, shiguchi, ari, kama, sen, shachi) that make good aliases next to English terms such as dovetail, gooseneck and draw-bore peg
usefulness.decision_support: None in the books or The Joinery beyond grouping by joint location. Tsugite gives live pass/fail feedback and suggestions for valid joints, which is a kind of design check but not a selector
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: The Joinery's animations were redrawn from the creator's collection of Japanese woodwork books (sources not named per joint), so they overlap with Sato and Nakahara and Seike. Seike is a translation of 'Kigumi'. Jochen Gros's 50 Digital Wood Joints (separate item) includes CNC versions modelled on Japanese joints (e.g. 'Ryo-men-ari-tsugi'). Tsugite overlaps with other HCI joint tools in the 'HCI fabrication research on joints' item (Zheng's Joinery tool) and with MiGumi (2025)
